# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) are a cornerstone of therapy for patients at risk of sudden cardiac death, with landmark trials such as MADIT-II, SCD-HeFT and AVID establishing their survival benefit in both primary and secondary prevention populations [1,2,3]. The majority of contemporary ICDs are implanted transvenously; however, this approach carries acute procedural and long-term risks, and the subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed, in part, to circumvent some of these adverse events or to serve as an alternative option in patients unable to undergo transvenous implantation [4]. The most frequent and clinically consequential complications of conventional systems involve the transvenous lead, motivating the design of an entirely extravascular alternative [5].

## Device design and implantation

ICDs prevent sudden death from cardiac causes in selected patients but require the use of transvenous lead systems; to eliminate the need for venous access, an entirely subcutaneous ICD system was designed and tested [5]. The system consists of a tripolar parasternal electrode connected to an electrically active pulse generator, with the electrode positioned parallel to and just left of the sternal midline and the generator positioned over the sixth rib between the midaxillary and anterior axillary lines [5]. A key practical advantage is that the S-ICD can be implanted by use of anatomic landmarks, obviating the need for fluoroscopy and thereby reducing radiation exposure for both the patient and physician [6].

A fundamental limitation, however, is the absence of pacing capability: although the S-ICD has demonstrated safety and efficacy for the treatment of malignant ventricular arrhythmias, a limitation lies in its inability to either pace-terminate ventricular tachycardia or provide prolonged bradycardia pacing support [7].

## Patient selection and screening

Because the S-ICD senses a surface-equivalent electrogram, candidates undergo mandatory electrocardiographic screening to minimise inappropriate shocks from T-wave oversensing. Approximately 8% of potential S-ICD patients are not eligible after failing the screening test, with patients showing T-wave inversions in leads I, II, and aVF being substantially more likely to fail [8]. Reported screening failure rates of 7–15% reflect the proportion of patients deemed ineligible based on QRS/T-wave morphology, often due to a low R:T ratio [9].

## Pivotal and registry evidence

The first pivotal investigation, an investigational device exemption trial, evaluated 314 patients. Using a prespecified 180-day complication-free performance goal of 79%, the trial supported the efficacy and safety of the S-ICD System for the treatment of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [10]. The EFFORTLESS registry extended these findings to nearly 1,000 patients; it remains the largest and longest follow-up study of S-ICD efficacy, demonstrating a high level of VT/VF shock efficacy over a median 5.1-year follow-up along with a low complication rate, very low conversion to transvenous devices, and few inappropriate shocks for atrial fibrillation or supraventricular tachycardia [11]. Notably, shock efficacy reached 98% at 5 years, and only about 2% of patients needed a transvenous device for pacing indications [11].

## Randomised comparisons with the transvenous ICD

The PRAETORIAN trial was the first randomised comparison in a general ICD population. Among patients with an indication for ICD therapy but not for pacing therapy, the subcutaneous ICD was noninferior to the transvenous ICD with respect to the cumulative incidence of the primary end point of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [12]. ICD-related complications were seen in 15.1% with an S-ICD versus 15.7% with a transvenous device after a median follow-up of 4 years, while lead complications occurred in 6.6% of transvenous patients compared with 1.4% of subcutaneous patients [12]. A prespecified secondary analysis confirmed that lead-related complications and systemic infections were more prevalent in the transvenous group, and complications in that group were more severe, requiring significantly more invasive interventions [13].

The ATLAS trial randomised younger and higher-risk patients. There was a statistically significant reduction in perioperative, lead-related complications, occurring in 1 patient (0.4%) with an S-ICD versus 12 patients (4.8%) with a transvenous ICD [14]. The S-ICD reduced perioperative, lead-related complications without significantly compromising shock effectiveness, but with more early postoperative pain and a trend toward more inappropriate shocks [14].

## Inappropriate shocks and programming

Inappropriate shocks—historically driven by T-wave oversensing—have been the principal drawback of the S-ICD, but contemporary programming and discrimination algorithms have markedly reduced them. In the UNTOUCHED trial, which enrolled primary-prevention patients with reduced ejection fraction, the inappropriate shock rate of 3.1% at 1 year was the lowest reported for the S-ICD and lower than many transvenous ICD studies using contemporary programming [15]. Meta-analytic data confirm that overall inappropriate-therapy rates are comparable between systems, though the mechanisms differ; inappropriate shock rates did not differ significantly between S-ICD and TV-ICD, with the S-ICD associated with a higher risk of cardiac oversensing offset by a higher risk of supraventricular arrhythmia–related shocks in the transvenous device [16].

## Defibrillation testing

Defibrillation testing at implant has been re-examined. The PRAETORIAN score, derived from device positioning on chest radiographs, was developed to predict defibrillation success and to potentially replace routine testing [17]. In the randomised PRAETORIAN-DFT trial, the rate of failed first shocks for spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias was 1.7% in the no-testing group and 2.3% in the testing group, meeting noninferiority criteria [18], suggesting testing can be safely omitted in optimally positioned systems.

## Complications and infection

Lead-related complications are consistently fewer with the S-ICD. A meta-analysis found significantly fewer lead complications in the S-ICD group, with a total infection rate of 0.35% among S-ICD recipients that was similar to the transvenous group [19]. The clinical relevance of avoiding intravascular hardware is underscored by the observation that the 1-year mortality of a device infection triples from 7% to 24% if the transvenous lead is involved [13].

## Future directions

The principal remaining gap—lack of pacing—is being addressed by modular systems pairing the S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker. One-year outcomes of the first modular pacing-defibrillator system revealed low system complication rates and good antitachycardia-pacing efficacy, suggesting modular cardiac rhythm management is a viable alternative to single-chamber ICDs without transvenous leads [20]; communication success between the S-ICD and leadless pacemaker was 98.8% [21].

## Guidelines and conclusion

Current guidelines endorse the S-ICD for appropriately selected patients. The 2022 ESC guidelines [22] and the 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS guidelines [23] both incorporate the S-ICD for patients without a pacing, resynchronisation, or antitachycardia-pacing indication. The high generator-change rate of the S-ICD does not translate into a higher risk of device-related complications, and the S-ICD should be considered for all ICD patients without an indication for pacing [24]. Supporting evidence spans the foundational human feasibility work [25], registry experience [26,27], programming refinements [28], real-world comparisons [29], and design rationale of randomised trials [30]. In summary, the S-ICD has matured from a niche device into a well-validated, guideline-endorsed alternative to the transvenous ICD, offering comparable efficacy with fewer lead-related complications for patients who do not require pacing.
